subject: Agriculture
title: Seed Banks and Genetic Vaults
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Seed Banks and Genetic Vaults.

hook.text: Deep inside an Arctic mountain, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores over 1.1 million seed samples from every country.

buildup.text: Crop wild relatives and ancient landraces carry genes for disease resistance, drought tolerance, and nutrition.

discovery.text: When the Syrian civil war destroyed Aleppo's seed bank, scientists recovered duplicates from Svalbard. The system worked.

twist.text: Climate change is warming the permafrost around Svalbard. The 'doomsday vault' itself faces its own climate threat.

climax.text: Without seed banks, crop improvement would lose irreplaceable raw material. They're agriculture's insurance policy.

punchline.text: A freezer in the Arctic guards the future of dinner.

quiz.question: What proved the Svalbard Seed Vault's worth?
options: Recovering seeds lost when Syria's Aleppo seed bank was destroyed by war

details.summary: Seed banks and genetic vaults preserve the diversity of crop varieties and wild relatives as insurance against future threats. This topic covers how seeds are collected, dried, and frozen at facilities worldwide to safeguard genetic resources for breeding.
details.whyItMatters: Modern agriculture relies on a dangerously narrow genetic base. Seed banks preserve the raw material breeders need to develop crops resistant to new diseases, pests, and climate conditions.
takeaways: Over 1,700 seed banks worldwide hold more than 7 million crop variety samples
Seeds are typically dried to low moisture and stored at minus 18 degrees Celsius
The Svalbard vault backs up collections from seed banks across 100+ countries

faq.question: How are seeds preserved in seed banks?
faq.answer: Seeds are cleaned, dried to about 5% moisture content, sealed in airtight foil packets, and stored in freezers at −18°C. Under these conditions, most crop seeds remain viable for decades or even centuries.

faq.question: Why is preserving crop genetic diversity so urgent?
faq.answer: Since the 1900s, about 75% of crop genetic diversity has been lost as farmers shifted to a few high-yielding varieties. Without preserved diversity, breeders lack the genetic raw material to develop crops adapted to future climate and disease threats.
